item.title: The Art of the Chinese Indirection: Why Silence Is the Most Elegant Insult of All
item.description: How Chinese indirection turned silence into a verbal weapon: history, examples, and the thousand-year-old logic of insulting without opening your mouth.
item.content:encoded:
There is an invisible hierarchy to human discontent. On the lowest step, shouting. Somewhere above it, the obvious comeback. At the top — where the air is thin and only the prepared ascend — stands silence. The Chinese indirection is the art of occupying that step without appearing to climb.

The silence that accuses

In the West we are taught that holding your tongue is losing. Silence implies consent, says the adage. The Chinese tradition runs the equation the other way: whoever talks too much gives themselves away. One of the most quoted episodes is Emperor Qianlong's answer to a bureaucrat who asked for a raise. There was no extended audience, no dramatic resignation. There was a short sentence, impeccably polite on its surface, which the official understood as a dismissal and the rest of the court understood as a masterpiece.

The mechanism is easy to describe and brutal to execute: the offensive message is assembled by whoever receives it. You supply the material, the interlocutor builds the insult, and the moral liability is theirs. It is a perfect indemnity policy: if the person takes offense, they have offended themselves.

Why it still works

Because social media invented the festival of instant replies, and indirection is the one jab that cannot be screenshotted. Hard to screenshot a silence. Hard to sue someone over what they didn't say. Chinese indirection has survived dynasties, cultural revolutions and algorithms because it depends on neither technology nor context: only on there being enough insecure people around to fill the gaps with their own fears.

There is also the aesthetic component. A well-made indirection is a sonnet: rigid form, sharpened content. Chinese proverbs condense discontent into four characters. The average Western insult needs three paragraphs, an unpronounceable adjective and a mention of your relatives. Economy of means is part of the insult.

How not to do it

The beginner's classic mistake is the sub-indirection: a message so veiled that nobody notices, target included. The Chinese indirection is not vague — it is too precise to be said out loud. The target knows. The audience suspects. The lawyers have no evidence. That triple equilibrium takes practice, which is why there is an entire literature on the subject, from imperial court letters to the family WhatsApp group, where the technique crossed the Pacific and adapted to local conditions with disconcerting ease.

Frequently asked questions

What is a Chinese indirection?

A criticism phrased so politely and so apparently neutral that the interlocutor is the one who builds — and suffers — the offense. The surface is courteous; the payload is terminal.

Can silence count as an insult?

In the logic of Chinese indirect communication, yes. Staying silent at the right moment signals disapproval more forcefully than any protest, and grants the other party the (dubious) honor of interpreting why.

Where can I read more about this?

The book The Art of the Chinese Indirection, by Clara Malcriada, gathers historical cases, proverbs and practical rules of the elegant offense — available on Amazon in Kindle format.

item.title: The Art of the Poisoned Compliment: When Praise Stings More Than an Insult
item.description: Compliments that wound: the Persian tradition of ta'arof, Arab blessings that work like plagues, and the fine engineering of taking the side door out.
item.content:encoded:
An insult is, deep down, an honest form of communication: it reports discontent, dated and signed. A compliment is more dangerous. In the Persian and Arab traditions — the world's two oldest schools of rhetorical contempt — the compliment is where civilization stores its worst intentions, with impeccable grammar.

The Persian school: praise until it hurts

Persia elevated the compliment to the status of a system. Ta'arof, the Iranian ritual of courtesy, consists of offering praise and refusals that nobody takes literally, a formal dance in which everyone lies elegantly and everyone knows it. It is the closest humanity has come to a bureaucracy of politeness. And, like every formal system, it produces lethal byproducts when someone decides to run the protocol in offensive mode.

The result is the compliment with the structure of a verdict. Praising someone's "courage" in the face of an evidently reckless decision. Celebrating the "originality" of an idea that was already proposed and rejected twice in the same month. Wishing the boss, publicly, that he "keep up this energy" on the day he calls the third meeting of the week to organize the other three.

The logic is the peacock's: splendid plumage, feet we would rather not see. The poisoned compliment displays the plumage out loud and leaves the feet to the listener. If the target reacts, they admit the cap fits. If they don't, the compliment hangs in the air for the audience's enjoyment. Either way, the author left through the side door — and the victim left through it too, shoved.

The Arab school: the blessing as plague

Arab rhetoric took the mechanism to another extreme: the blessing that curses. The Arab tradition of literary cursing — a genre with centuries of résumé — discovered early that a courteous wish devastates more than an open plague, because it cannot be contested without the contesting party confessing.

Anthological example: wishing someone "patience" in public. Surface: a vote of moral strength. Content: an official declaration that the person has insoluble problems and is the cause of them. Saying someone "has the soul of a child" sounds like tenderness; operated correctly, it is a diagnosis of consequence. Congratulating a "well-deserved achievement" with the stress on deserved turns the dinner table into a court of audit.

The Persian tradition closes the circle with its gift for symptom: "the crow that learned to walk like the partridge forgot how it used to walk". Praise the imitator for their "versatility" and the sentence does all the work on its own.

How to tell a compliment from a verdict

Three signs. First: a real compliment speaks of something concrete you did; a poisoned one speaks of one of your qualities in the abstract, usually one nobody had confirmed yet. Second: an honest compliment ends; a poisoned one comes with follow-up — the "keep it up", the "everyone's been saying", the add-on that hooks an expectation onto the praise. Third: the honest compliment survives your absence; the poisoned one needs witnesses.

Once the poison is confirmed, the classic reply is to thank twice — the second time, for "such care with my development". That is the school handing the shovel back.

Some consider all of this cruelty dressed as literature. It is literature dressed as courtesy — and the difference matters less than the aim.

Frequently asked questions

What is ta'arof?

The Iranian formal system of courtesy: ritual praise, invitations and refusals that nobody interprets literally. Operated with offensive intent, it becomes the most polite vehicle for humiliation in the world.

How can a compliment offend more than an insult?

An insult can be contested, since it accuses in the author's name. The poisoned compliment leaves the offense open: whoever reacts looks paranoid, whoever swallows it has no defense. The Persian and Arab traditions have exploited that asymmetry for centuries.

Where can I read more about Persian and Arab insults?

In the books The Art of the Persian Insult and Arabic Insults, by Clara Malcriada — both available on Amazon in Kindle format.

item.title: How to Insult with Elegance: A Guide to The Art of Insults Series
item.description: A comparative guide to The Art of Insults: the Chinese, Russian, Arab and Persian traditions — which book to start with and what each one teaches.
item.content:encoded:
Insulting well is a trade. Insulting with elegance is a discipline with a curriculum, and The Art of Insults is, at the moment, the field's only unofficial graduate program. Four volumes, four ancient traditions and one principle: the perfect insult leaves no bruise — it leaves reflection.

The four schools

The Art of the Chinese Indirection is the school of subtext. Its central thesis: the best offense is the one the target assembles alone, from material you merely left on the floor. Maximum compression, zero drama. Recommended for anyone surrounded by people who take offense in advance.

Russian Insults is the school of density. The Russian insult carries history, irony and prognosis in the same sentence — it offends in the present and in the past, and reserves a blow for the interlocutor's future. Recommended for anyone who believes a jab should require at least two readings.

Arabic Insults is the school of rhetoric. Here contempt is a literary genre: parlor curses, marketplace plagues and proverbs that disqualify the adversary with grammatical precision. Recommended for anyone convinced that offending is, above all, a matter of command of the language.

The Art of the Persian Insult is the school of metaphor. The Iranian tradition criticizes the way Hafez wrote: in verse, with flowers, and a thorn in the center. It is the most beautiful insult in the repertoire — the kind the victim frames before realizing they were the target. For those who want to humiliate with aesthetics, and be applauded for it.

In what order to read

There is no official order, but there is a pedagogical one. Start with the Chinese indirection (the foundation: less is more). Move on to the Russian insults (the deepening: density and context). Then the Arabic insults (the technique: rhetoric and register). Close with the Persian insult (the mastery: metaphor and form). It is the same progression as any craft: measure first, cut second, dance last.

What the series is not

It is not a manual of aggression. None of the four volumes teaches shouting, public humiliation or answering your boss on the corporate email thread. The series rests on the premise that verbal violence is the symptom of an undersized vocabulary, and that whoever has range does not need volume. If you are looking for ready-made insults to screenshot, this is not your program. If you are looking for sharp arguments dressed as civility, welcome.

Frequently asked questions

Which book of The Art of Insults should I read first?

Russian Insults is the most self-contained for new readers; The Art of the Chinese Indirection is the shortest and doubles as an introduction to the method. Any of the four works as an entry point.

Do the books teach insults?

No. The series teaches rhetoric, irony and elegant criticism drawn from literary traditions — no direct aggression, no gratuitous swearing.

Are all the books on Amazon?

Yes. The four volumes of the series are available on Amazon in Kindle format, and most are included in the Kindle Unlimited program.

item.title: 7 Chinese Indirections That Fit in a WhatsApp Message
item.description: Seven Chinese indirections ready for the family group chat: thousand-year-old proverbs that offend with courtesy, fit in one message, and leave nothing to screenshot.
item.content:encoded:
The imperial court of Beijing and the family WhatsApp group have more in common than their headcount. In both, whoever talks too much loses. In both, information circulates in circles. And in both, whoever plays badly is handled with a courtesy so impeccable it takes days to hurt. The difference is that the imperial court, at least, deigned to justify its own rules.

For two thousand years the Chinese tradition of communicating discontent by indirection has produced exactly the material the West invented late, for the medium it invented late. Short proverbs, polite surface, terminal content. Seven of them — field-tested and approved by entire dynasties — fit in a single message:

  1. Playing the zither to a buffalo (对牛弹琴). For when you have explained something three times and the person replies with a question that was already answered. Send the proverb. The buffalo will spend a while trying to figure out what it means — which confirms the diagnosis.
  2. Lifting a rock to drop it on your own foot (搬起石头砸自己的脚). The standard reply to whoever criticized your work and then showed up with the same error signed beneath their own name.
  3. The blind men feeling the elephant (盲人摸象). For the meeting in which each participant drew a radical conclusion from a different corner of the problem and the three reports contradict each other.
  4. Water too clean holds no fish (水至清则无鱼). For the perfectionist colleague who returned the report with nine comments on the italics and zero on the content. Excessive rigidity drives people away; the proverb warns with the sweetness of an aquarium.
  5. The rumor dies in the ear of the wise (谣言止于智者). For the relative who forwards a scam chain message captioned "just checking this with you all". It closes the topic and the sender's standing in the same line.
  6. A knife hidden in the smile (笑里藏刀). The proverb here is an instruction for use, a message: it is the school of the "haha how great!!" with two exclamation marks, addressed to whoever has just announced in the group that your idea was wonderful — after trying to bury it in the hallway.
  7. The more words, the more mistakes (言多必失). For the ten-minute voice note. It works as a philosophical reminder for the other members of the group and as a sentence for the author.

The mechanism that makes all of this work in a group chat is the same that made it work in imperial correspondence: the offensive message is assembled by whoever receives it. You deliver first-rate historical material, the person translates it, and when the penny drops — sometimes days later, in the middle of dinner — the only witness is themselves. A screenshot proves what was written; it does not prove what was understood.

There is also a class advantage: answering with a two-thousand-year-old proverb repositions the argument on a different plane of gravity. The opponent argues; you cite. It is the difference between yelling at the market and asking the waiter for another bottle. Whoever is answered with a Chinese proverb understands, at once, that the conversation has changed register — and that the new register is higher and poorly lit.

It works with the mother-in-law, with the boss and with that relative who asks in the group when you will finally get a proper job. In these cases, the proverb is not sophistication: it is philanthropy.

Frequently asked questions

What is a Chinese indirection?

A criticism with a polite surface and a sharpened payload, in which the interlocutor assembles the offense and therefore suffers it. The Chinese tradition documented the practice two thousand years ago in proverbs, letters and court anecdotes.

How do I answer an irritating message without starting a fight?

With an indirect proverb, in the vein of "playing the zither to a buffalo" or "the rumor dies in the ear of the wise". The message stays polite, the point lands, and the exchange produces no case law in the group.

Where can I study more Chinese indirections?

In the book The Art of the Chinese Indirection, by Clara Malcriada, which gathers proverbs, historical cases and guides for use — available on Amazon in Kindle format.

item.title: Insults That Became Proverbs: What History Approved
item.description: Every proverb with an edge is an insult that passed centuries of review: the Russian filter of censorship and the Chinese filter of compression, with examples.
item.content:encoded:
Most offenses die the day they are born. A few survive a generation, like a fire hydrant in a warehouse. And a handful cross centuries of wars, censors and spelling reforms to reach the status of proverb — the insult with a seal of quality, approved by a review committee composed of every dead speaker of the language.

Getting past that committee is the most rigorous selection process in the history of discontent. Russia and China, two traditions that treated the proverb as a literary genre, show what it demands.

The Russian filter: censorship as publisher

A country where complaining out loud cost you dearly for four hundred years developed a language edited by survival. What circulated was the short, the dense and the hard to punish. The result sits in the collection of Russian proverbs, where censorship functions as a merciless publisher: nothing mediocre survives four centuries of copyediting.

Consider the quality bar. "Strength is enough — brains are unnecessary" (Сила есть — ума не надо) is a seven-word phrase that has been disqualifying bosses, governments and brothers-in-law since before the invention of the boss, the government and the brother-in-law. "Every wading bird praises its own swamp" (Всяк кулик своё болото хвалит) settles, in one image, every case of self-promotion since the invention of self-promotion. And "Had I known the cards, I'd live in Sochi" (Знал бы прикуп, жил бы в Сочи) is the definitive answer to whoever attributes other people's success to insider information — a jab that survived the empire, the revolution and the Soviet Union, and still has energy left over for the betting market.

Density is the admission criterion. The Russian insult approved by history carries diagnosis, irony and prognosis in the same sentence, and keeps working when applied to situations its authors never lived to see. That is the test: a good proverb must be able to offend people not born yet.

The Chinese filter: two thousand years of compression

The Chinese tradition applied an engineer's standard to the insult: maximum effect per unit of material. Four-character proverbs deliver an entire critique, termination clause included.

"Playing the zither to a buffalo" (对牛弹琴) eliminates an entire alignment meeting with one image. "Lifting a rock to drop it on your own foot" (搬起石头砸自己的脚) forecasts consequences with the precision of an insurance company. "Water too clean holds no fish" (水至清则无鱼) executes the toxic perfectionist and throws in, free of charge, a lesson in people management. And "the more words, the more mistakes" (言多必失) is the oldest traffic warning still in force.

The Chinese committee has one extra criterion: the indirection. The approved proverb never accuses in its own name — it supplies the material and lets the target assemble the offense, which thus arrives pre-assembled, signed and without appeal.

What the approved ones have in common

Three attributes: extreme compression, no expiration date, and a target who identifies themselves. A proverb that becomes a jab does not describe a person; it describes a category, and the person joins it of their own accord. That is why they cross dynasties and income brackets: the imperial bureaucracy and the regional manager belong to the same taxonomic subspecies, and the proverb knew it all along.

History, in the end, approved what deserved approval. Languages kept centuries of offenses in permanent circulation and discarded everything that required volume. Whoever doubts it can run the experiment at home: try insulting someone with a long paragraph and see how much of the sentence is left after a week.

Frequently asked questions

Which Russian proverbs work as elegant insults?

"Strength is enough — brains are unnecessary", "every wading bird praises its own swamp" and "Had I known the cards, I'd live in Sochi" are classic examples, commented with historical context in the book Russian Insults.

What is the difference between a Chinese and a Russian proverb?

The Russian favors density: irony, history and prognosis in one sentence. The Chinese favors compression and indirection: four characters that deliver the critique and leave the target to finish the offense alone.

Where can I read more about proverbs that offend?

In Russian Insults and The Art of the Chinese Indirection, by Clara Malcriada — both available on Amazon in Kindle format.

item.title: Malcriada Books: editing and publishing for authors
item.description: Malcriada Books is open to authors who already have a manuscript and need help with editing, formats, metadata and publishing on Amazon.
item.content:encoded:
Some people write. Others want to write but get stuck in the boring part: formatting, picking keywords, uploading the file to Amazon, waiting for review and trying to understand the reports. Malcriada Books is for that second part.

We do not write your book for you. You bring the text, we take it to the shelf.

What we do

We read the manuscript and point out what needs fixing. Then come line editing and chapter structure, followed by the ebook and the hardcover. The cover is prepared at the right size for the chosen paper, with the spine calculated from the real page count.

For publication, we put together title, subtitle, description, categories and keywords. The KDP upload and submission for review are part of the job too. Once the book is live, we track KENP and sales so we can adjust the positioning.

How it works in practice

The first step is a simple conversation: what the book is about, which language it will be published in and where you want to sell it. From there we agree on a scope and a deadline. We do not promise sales miracles. We promise the right file, in the right format, with solid metadata.

If you already have a finished book and like what you see here, the door is open. Use the contact form and tell us a bit about the project.

Frequently asked questions

Do you write the book?

No. The text is yours. We work on what you already wrote: editing, formatting, cover, metadata and publishing.

Which languages do you publish in?

Portuguese and English. The language sets the store, the metadata and the keyword strategy.

How long does it take?

It depends on the state of the manuscript and the queue. After the first conversation, you get a scope with an agreed deadline.

item.title: How to Answer Without Answering: The Manual of the Eloquent Silence
item.description: A practical manual of the eloquent silence: five techniques for answering without answering, drawn from the Chinese, Russian and Persian traditions.
item.content:encoded:
There is one question that crosses every era and every class: how to answer what does not deserve an answer, without forfeiting your turn? The great traditions of rhetorical contempt — Chinese, Russian, Arab and Persian — arrived, separated by continents and centuries, at the same technical conclusion: the best answer is the one that does not look like one.

The eloquent silence is not the absence of a reply. It is a reply whose grammar refuses to register. Instructions for use:

The five techniques

1. The refused tea. In Russian houses, refusing the tea that was offered is a complete social sentence — no words need accompany it. The contemporary version is the read receipt: read the offensive message and do not reply. The message was received, registered and judged. The sender is left with the hard part, which is finding out the verdict.

2. Thanks for services not rendered. A Persian technique, documented in the survival repertoire of government offices: whoever spent the day shuffled from desk to desk thanks the last bureaucrat for the "invaluable lesson" in patience. Apply it to the boss who delayed your project: "thank you for the opportunity to learn how to wait". They can thank their own incompetence on your behalf.

3. The shovel returned as a question. The jewel of the Persian school: hand the adversary back, with every courtesy, the shovel with which they will dig their own grave. "One honest question: which variable changed since the last time this failed?" There is no good answer. Every attempt at justification is the adversary reading the verdict aloud.

4. The smile with a knife. Chinese school, official proverb: 笑里藏刀, the knife hidden in the smile. Applaud someone's joke with a measured "haha, funny" — no content, no double exclamation, no follow-up. The conversation ends there, and the interlocutor leaves looking for the cut, never finding the blade.

5. The ritual delay. Answer, two days later, with one short neutral sentence, what was delivered in a three-minute voice note. The delay communicates that the matter went through a review committee; the short sentence communicates the outcome. Russian format: dense in the past, dry in the present, terminal in the future.

Safety rules

The eloquent silence requires an investment: it only works on people who expect a reply. Staying silent before someone who never noticed is mere isolation. The target must be anticipating your answer — then, and only then, does silence become a sentence and delay become a tribunal.

Second rule: the silence must be signed. Any silence is vague; the eloquent one needs a frame — the read receipt with knowledge of its effects, the "noted" followed by a "thanks" that thanks nothing, the elegant exit from the group with two proverbs' notice. The Chinese school calls this supplying the material and letting the other build the offense; it is called that because that is exactly what happens.

Third: there are situations in which the direct answer is mandatory — threats, abuse, contracts. The eloquent silence operates where civilization allows; where it does not, the undersized vocabulary becomes acceptable again.

Frequently asked questions

What is the eloquent silence?

A reply that refuses to formally manifest itself: the framed non-answer — the delayed read receipt, the ironic thank-you, the ceremonious exit — which communicates judgment more forcefully than any retort.

Does answering without answering work at work?

With restraint: it works with colleagues and superiors who expect your reaction, and fails on whoever never noticed. The Persian (the question returned as a shovel) and Russian (the ritual delay) techniques are the safest in a corporate setting.

Where can I study the traditions behind these techniques?

In The Art of Insults series, by Clara Malcriada — four volumes on the Chinese, Russian, Arab and Persian traditions, all available on Amazon in Kindle format.

item.title: Russian Insults: 7 Classic Put-Downs That Outlived the Tsars
item.description: Seven classic insults of the Russian tradition that outlived tsars, soviets and memes — and what they reveal about offending with elegance.
item.content:encoded:
Russia produced, in strict historical sequence, the world's greatest novels, the world's worst winters, and a tradition of insult that manages to be poetic and terminal at the same time. No coincidence: a country where talking too much was once grounds for exile developed the ability to say everything with a minimum of words and a maximum of consequence.

What makes an insult outlive the tsars

An insult is like an eraser: most of them wear out on first use. The Russian classics survived because they operate in layers. On the surface, an almost polite observation. In the next layer, a comparison that humiliates. In the deep layer, a truth about the person that the person preferred to ignore. It is insult in layers: the longer you chew, the worse it gets.

Seven examples survived the empire, the revolution, the Soviet Union and the meme era — if they crossed all of that, they must be built to last:

  1. The comparison with the bureaucracy: being called an "office rubber stamp" is to be accused of official uselessness, with seal and signature.
  2. The climate jab: invoking the Russian winter as a metaphor for the interlocutor's character. Cold, long, with no hope of ending.
  3. The inverted compliment: congratulating someone on a quality the person does not have. The oldest documented form of sarcasm and still the most effective.
  4. The literary reference: quoting Gogol or Dostoevsky in an offensive context turns humiliation into a seminar. The victim leaves the conversation with a wound and a reading list.
  5. The silence with tea: refusing the tea that was offered is, in certain houses, a complete social sentence. Not a single word required.
  6. The polite lie: saying "thank you for your opinion" in the right intonation is the equivalent of a criminal proceeding.
  7. The underrated praise of perseverance: saying that someone "insists like Peter the Great besieging Narva" acknowledges effort and predicts failure in the same sentence.

Why the tradition survived

Because the Russian insult was never about aggression — it was about density. A Russian jab offends in the interlocutor's present, past and future. It is the only form of offense that makes the offended party work to process it, which explains why so many people only understand the blow on the way home, at three in the morning.

And there is the political survival factor. Under regimes where complaining out loud was expensive, irony became infrastructure. The classic put-downs circulated in salons, letters and kitchens — always in the densest and least punishable format. The result is a repertoire edited by centuries of censorship — and nobody proofreads a language with more rigor.

Frequently asked questions

What are the most famous classic Russian insults?

Comparisons with the imperial bureaucracy, inverted compliments, references to Gogol and Dostoevsky, and the ceremonious silence before the offered tea — all listed and contextualized in the book Russian Insults.

Why are Russian insults considered elegant?

Because they are dense and indirect: they carry irony, historical context and prognosis in few words, and offend without explicit aggression or grounds for an immediate comeback.

Where can I read more about the art of insulting in Russian?

Russian Insults, by Clara Malcriada, explores the tradition from the tsars to the present day, with commented examples — available on Amazon in Kindle format.

item.title: When Irony Becomes Art: Who Is Clara Malcriada
item.description: Who is Clara Malcriada, author of The Art of Insults: the project of rescuing the Chinese, Russian, Arab and Persian traditions of the elegant insult.
item.content:encoded:
The name explains the project. "Clara" is what one expects of a writer: clarity, method, bibliography. "Malcriada" — Portuguese for badly raised, unmannered — is what the bibliography produces. Between the two words lies an entire course of reading: someone who studied the great rhetorical traditions of the world in earnest and concluded, to the enormous disappointment of the curriculum, that humanity perfected the insult before perfecting nearly anything else.

The project

Clara Malcriada is a Brazilian author of sarcastic books on insults, irony and elegant verbal comebacks. Her work starts from an uncomfortable thesis: every civilization developed, before the internet, a complete system of refined discontent — and what the internet did was dump that patrimony onto a platform where nobody has more repertoire than urgency.

The Art of Insults recovers these systems one by one. About Clara Malcriada holds the full inventory; the summary is as follows:

The Art of the Chinese Indirection documents the school of subtext: two thousand years of proverbs, letters and court anecdotes teaching the offense whose assembly is the target's job. Maximum compression, zero drama, patrimony certified by dynasties.

Russian Insults covers the school of density: a country where complaining out loud cost you dearly for centuries produced insults that carry irony, history and prognosis in one sentence. Tsars, revolutions and memes evaluated the material; it passed every exam.

Arabic Insults organizes the school of rhetoric: parlor curses, blessings that work like plagues and proverbs of grammatical disqualification — the tradition that discovered the courteous wish offends more than the open plague.

The Art of the Persian Insult closes the series with the school of metaphor: the Iranian tradition criticizes the way Hafez wrote, with flowers and a thorn in the center. It is the most beautiful insult in the world repertoire — the kind the victim frames before realizing they were the target.

The method

Each volume follows the protocol of an academic research project without the academy's authorization: historical sources, context, commented examples and guides for contemporary application. The books do not teach shouting — they teach building. The editorial premise is that verbal aggression is the symptom of an undersized vocabulary, and that whoever mastered the repertoire never needed volume.

The reader who arrives at this blog through a search engine is generally after one of three things: an indirection for the family group chat, an answer to a ten-minute voice note, or an explanation of why they are still thinking about what they should have said in the meeting. The posts try to solve the immediate; the books solve the structural.

Irony is called art when it outlives its author. These traditions outlived their authors, their censors and their dynasties — and now have, for the first time in English as well as Portuguese, an organized catalog. Be it said in defense of civilization: it always knew how to insult well. What was missing was someone to catalog it. And someone willing to sign the catalog with a name that admits the trade out loud: clear in method, unmannered in intent.

Frequently asked questions

Who is Clara Malcriada?

A Brazilian author of sarcastic books on insults, irony and elegant verbal comebacks, specialized in the Chinese, Russian, Arab and Persian traditions of refined criticism. Full biography and catalog on the about page.

Which book of The Art of Insults should I read first?

Russian Insults works well as an entry point for new readers; The Art of the Chinese Indirection is the shortest and introduces the series' method. The next two, Arabic Insults and The Art of the Persian Insult, deepen rhetoric and metaphor.

Where can I buy Clara Malcriada's books?

All titles are available on Amazon in Kindle format, and most are included in the Kindle Unlimited program — links in every blog post and on the about page.
